title: How many continuing education hours do insurance adjusters need in Texas?
description: Texas adjuster CE: 24 hours every 2 years with ethics and classroom minimums, late fines, exemptions and DHS adjuster rules under 28 TAC Chapter 19.
shortAnswer: Texas requires licensed insurance adjusters to complete 24 hours of continuing education in each two-year license period. The Texas Department of Insurance (TDI) states that at least 12 hours must be classroom or classroom equivalent and 3 hours must be ethics. Hours must be finished before midnight Central Time on the expiration date, or TDI fines $50 per missing hour, capped at $500 per license type.
keyTakeaways: 28 Texas Administrative Code section 19.1003(a) sets 24 hours of CE per license and reporting period for most licensees, including adjusters, with at least 50% in certified classroom or classroom equivalent courses.

TDI's adjuster guidance requires 3 ethics hours for licenses expiring after August 31, 2022 (2 hours before that); the rule text published in section 19.1003 still contains a two hour reference, so check the current Texas Register text.
Excess hours cannot be carried forward, and hours earned before the license was issued generally do not count (section 19.1003(a)(2)).
Texas designated home state (DHS) adjusters must meet the same CE as resident adjusters (section 19.1003(e)); most nonresidents follow their home state's rules instead.
Licensees continuously licensed by TDI for at least 20 years, with no lapse over 90 days, can qualify for an exemption under section 19.1004(c), but only after TDI confirms it in writing.
regulator: Texas Department of Insurance (TDI), under the Texas Insurance Code and Title 28, Chapter 19, Subchapter K of the Texas Administrative Code
appliesTo: Resident all-lines, property and casualty, and workers' compensation adjusters licensed by TDI
Designated home state adjusters who designate Texas as their home state
Nonresident adjusters whose home state has no CE requirement
Employers and carriers that rely on licensed adjusters, and CE providers registered with TDI

sections.heading: How many CE hours does a Texas adjuster need?

blocks.text: A Texas adjuster needs 24 hours of continuing education every two years, completed within the license term. TDI's [all-lines adjuster license management page](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/agent/adjuster-all-lines-manage.html) states the requirement directly, and the underlying rule is [28 TAC section 19.1003](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/texas/28-Tex-Admin-Code-SS-19-1003), as at November 2026.

items: **Total:** 24 hours per license and reporting period (section 19.1003(a)). A 10 hour requirement applies only to certain limited agent licenses, not to adjusters.
**Delivery mix:** at least 50% of required hours, which is 12 of 24, in certified classroom or classroom equivalent courses (section 19.1003(a)(1)(C)); TDI's page states the same 12 hour minimum.
**Ethics:** TDI states that 3 hours must be in ethics, and that licenses that expired on or before August 31, 2022 needed only 2.
**Remainder:** completed through certified courses applicable to any license type (section 19.1003(a)(1)(D)).

**Multiple licenses:** a person holding several TDI licenses completes no more than the hours of the greatest single license requirement, three of which must be certified ethics or consumer protection hours (section 19.1003(b)).

blocks.title: Check the ethics hour count
blocks.text: TDI's adjuster guidance says three ethics hours. The text of 28 TAC section 19.1003(a)(1)(B), as republished by the Legal Information Institute, still says "at least two hours" of certified ethics or consumer protection, while section 19.1003(b) refers to three. Plan for three hours, and confirm against the current official text before relying on the lower figure.

sections.heading: What happens if an adjuster misses the deadline?

blocks.text: TDI fines $50 for each hour not completed before midnight Central Time on the license expiration date, with no exceptions, and will not renew the license until hours and fines are both cleared. For licenses that expired after June 1, 2018, the fine is capped at $500 per license type.

Paying a fine does not remove the course requirement: the missing hours must still be completed. Paid fines are non-refundable, even if an exemption or extension is granted later. TDI recommends finishing hours at least 30 days before expiration so providers have time to report completions. The renewal fee is $50, with a $25 late fee if it is not paid before midnight Central Time on the expiration date.

Section 19.1003(a)(2)(C) also blocks double counting: hours completed to cure a shortfall from a previous period under Insurance Code section 4004.055 do not count toward the current period. A [refresh cycle](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles) that targets completion well before the expiration date avoids both the fine and the double-booking problem.

sections.heading: Which hours do not count toward Texas adjuster CE?

blocks.text: Hours completed outside the current license period generally do not count. Section 19.1003(a)(2) denies credit for courses taken before TDI issued the license, including those taken under a temporary license or provisional permit, and bars carrying excess hours forward to the next period.

There are two narrow exceptions to the pre-license rule: a certified flood insurance course taken within the 12 months before licensing under section 19.1021, and the DHS adjuster conversion rules in section 19.1003(e). Prorated periods also change the count: under section 19.1003(d), a licensee whose license term is shorter than two years, or who converts from nonresident to resident, owes one hour per whole month remaining in the period, and owes nothing if the prorated period is under six months. DHS adjusters do not qualify for this proration.

sections.heading: Do nonresident and designated home state adjusters follow Texas rules?

blocks.text: Nonresidents usually follow their home state's CE rules, but DHS adjusters who designate Texas must follow Texas rules exactly as a resident would. TDI states that a nonresident whose home state does not require CE must follow Texas rules.

Section 19.1003(e) requires a Texas DHS adjuster to complete CE under the same requirements as a Texas resident adjuster. A DHS adjuster who converts to a resident license during the period must complete CE as a resident for the combined period and cannot use proration. This matters for catastrophe adjusters who live in states without adjuster licensing and use Texas as their designated home state.
Yes, but both require an application before the license expires. TDI says requests for an extension or a 20 year exemption must be submitted at least two weeks before the expiration date.

items: **20 year exemption:** under [28 TAC section 19.1004(c)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/texas/28-Tex-Admin-Code-SS-19-1004), a licensee continuously licensed by TDI for at least 20 years on or after January 1, 2003 is exempt from the hour requirement. "Continuously licensed" means no lapse over 90 days. The exemption begins in the reporting period in which the 20th year is reached, and may not be claimed before TDI's written notice.
**Scope:** any exemption or extension applies to all license types the person holds, and TDI may audit to confirm the qualifying circumstances still exist (section 19.1004(a)).

**Not a full release:** the 20 year exemption does not cover separate certification requirements such as the long-term care partnership CE in section 19.1023, which applies to agents rather than adjusters.

sections.heading: How does adjuster prelicensing education relate to CE?

blocks.text: Prelicensing education is an alternative to the licensing exam, not a substitute for CE. Under section 19.1003(c), an applicant seeking the exam exemption in Insurance Code section 4101.056(a)(4) must complete a certified adjuster prelicensing course of at least 40 hours, with at least 30 hours classroom or classroom equivalent, and pass the course exam. Once licensed, the 24 hour CE cycle starts.

Claims handling competence in other markets is regulated differently. Australia, for example, relies on industry code and licensee obligations, described on the page on [general insurance claims handling training](/regulations/general-insurance-claims-handling-training). Florida's adjuster rules are on the page on [Florida insurance adjuster continuing education](/regulations/florida-insurance-adjuster-continuing-education).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry records Texas hour categories, ethics minimums and DHS rules as separate obligations attached to each adjuster role and license. Claims procedures and ethics content map to those obligations, so firms see coverage by requirement rather than by course title.

faqs.q: Can online courses count as classroom hours in Texas?
faqs.a: Some can. Section 19.1003(a)(1)(C) refers to classroom or classroom equivalent courses, and TDI certifies how each course is classified. An adjuster should check the course classification in Sircon's approved course inquiry before relying on an online course toward the 12 hour minimum.

faqs.q: Do I need Texas CE if I hold a Texas nonresident adjuster license?
faqs.a: Usually not. TDI says nonresidents follow their home state's rules, unless the home state has no CE requirement. If you hold a Texas designated home state adjuster license, you must follow Texas rules exactly as a resident adjuster does, under section 19.1003(e).

faqs.q: Can I carry extra hours into my next license period?
faqs.a: No. Section 19.1003(a)(2)(B) denies credit for excess hours carried forward from one reporting period to the next. Hours must be earned within the current two-year term, so completing far more than 24 hours in one term does not reduce the next term's requirement.

faqs.q: How do I check how many hours I have?
faqs.a: TDI directs licensees to the Sircon website's Continuing Education Transcript Inquiry, which shows hours reported by providers. Because providers need time to report, TDI recommends completing hours at least 30 days before the license expires.

factCheck.claim: TDI all-lines adjuster page (last updated 11/2/2026): 24 hours of CE every two years; at least 12 hours classroom or classroom equivalent; three hours ethics, two if license expired on or before August 31, 2022; complete 30 days before expiry recommended.

TDI: $50 fine per hour not completed before midnight CT on expiration date; maximum $500 per license type for licenses expiring after June 1, 2018; fines non-refundable and do not relieve course requirement; renewal fee $50 and $25 late fee; nonresidents follow home state unless no CE; Texas DHS follows Texas rules; extension and 20 year exemption requests two weeks before expiry.

28 TAC 19.1003(a): 24 hours per license and reporting period (10 for specified limited licenses); (a)(1)(B) at least two hours ethics or consumer protection; (a)(1)(C) at least 50% classroom or classroom equivalent; (a)(2) no credit before license issued, no carry forward, no double counting of 4004.055 shortfall hours; (b) greatest single license requirement with three hours ethics or consumer protection.

28 TAC 19.1003(c) adjuster prelicensing course of at least 40 hours with at least 30 classroom hours for exam exemption under Insurance Code 4101.056(a)(4); (d) proration one hour per whole month, none if under six months, excluding Texas DHS adjusters; (e) Texas DHS adjusters complete CE as resident adjusters.

28 TAC 19.1004(a) exemptions and extensions apply to all license types and TDI may audit; (c) 20 years continuous licensure on or after January 1, 2003, no lapse over 90 days, written notice required before claiming.
28 TAC 19.1021(d) and (e): flood insurance course may be taken within 12 months preceding license issue and count up to three hours toward the initial CE requirement.
